title: Conjecture 1.3 (Lee)
statement_text: Let $d$ be sufficiently large, let $G$ be a connected graph with $n$ vertices and minimum degree at least $d$, and let $\mathcal{T}$ be a uniformly random spanning tree of $G$. Then, for every tree $T$ it holds that $$\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{T}\cong T)\leq n^{-\Omega(1)}.$$
context_text: Lee conjectured that a polynomial anticoncentration property should hold for random spanning trees in graphs with large minimum degree, motivated by the complete bipartite graph $K_{d,n-d}$ having only $n^{\mathcal{O}(d)}$ non-isomorphic spanning trees despite having large minimum degree. The methods of Lee's earlier work do not yield a proof, as they rely on counting embeddings in almost regular graphs and cannot produce polynomial-only bounds.
paper_contribution: Proves the conjecture in a strong form: for every connected graph $G$ with $n$ vertices and minimum degree at least $d$, and every tree $T$, $\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{T}\cong T)\leq n^{-\Omega(d)}$, with the exponent growing linearly in $d$.

title: Conjecture 4.1
statement_text: Let $d$ be sufficiently large, and let $n$ be sufficiently large relative to $d$. Suppose that $G$ is a connected graph with $n$ vertices and minimum degree at least $d$, and let $\mathcal{T}$ be a uniformly random spanning tree of $G$. Then, for every tree $T$ it holds that $$\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{T}\cong T)\leq n^{-(1/2-o_n(1))(d-1)}.$$
context_text: A uniformly random spanning tree $\mathcal{T}$ of $G$ is chosen uniformly among all spanning trees, and $\mathcal{T}\cong T$ means isomorphic as unlabeled trees; two spanning trees are non-isomorphic if they are not isomorphic as abstract trees. Lee showed that almost regular graphs of large degree $d$ have $e^{\Omega(n)}$ non-isomorphic spanning trees, via the anticoncentration bound $\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{T}\cong T)\le e^{-\Omega(n)}$, and conjectured that minimum degree $d$ (large) gives at least $\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{T}\cong T)\le n^{-\Omega(1)}$; exponential bounds are impossible since $K_{d,n-d}$ has only $n^{O(d)}$ non-isomorphic spanning trees. The authors prove Lee's conjecture in a strong form: for $d$ large, $n$ large relative to $d$, and $G$ connected with $n$ vertices and minimum degree at least $d$, $\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{T}\cong T)\le n^{-\Omega(d)}$ for every tree $T$, hence $G$ has at least $n^{\Omega(d)}$ non-isomorphic spanning trees; this is optimal up to the constant in the exponent. The conjecture asks for the optimal constant $1/2$, which would match $K_{d,n-d}$: up to isomorphism, a spanning tree of $K_{d,n-d}$ is determined by a minimal subtree connecting the $d$ vertices of the small class (boundedly many configurations) and the numbers of leaves attached to these $d$ vertices, which in a uniformly random spanning tree follow a multinomial distribution with $n-O(d)$ trials and probabilities $1/d$; hence some isomorphism class has probability $\Omega(n^{-(d-1)/2})$.
notes: The full inequality in the statement was not explicitly reproduced in the extracted theorem block; the bound $n^{-(1/2-o_n(1))(d-1)}$ is inferred from the context text which states the optimal constant should be $1/2$ and that this would match $K_{d,n-d}$.

title: Conjecture 4.2
statement_text: Let $d$ be sufficiently large, and let $n$ be sufficiently large relative to $d$. Suppose that $G$ is a connected graph with $n$ vertices and minimum degree at least $d$. Then, the number of non-isomorphic spanning trees of $G$ is at least $\Omega(n^{d-1})$.
context_text: A uniformly random spanning tree $\mathcal{T}$ of $G$ is chosen uniformly among all spanning trees, and $\mathcal{T}\cong T$ means isomorphic as unlabeled trees; two spanning trees are non-isomorphic if they are not isomorphic as abstract trees. Lee showed that almost regular graphs of large degree $d$ have $e^{\Omega(n)}$ non-isomorphic spanning trees, via the anticoncentration bound $\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{T}\cong T)\le e^{-\Omega(n)}$, and conjectured that minimum degree $d$ (large) gives at least $\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{T}\cong T)\le n^{-\Omega(1)}$; exponential bounds are impossible since $K_{d,n-d}$ has only $n^{O(d)}$ non-isomorphic spanning trees. The authors prove Lee's conjecture in a strong form: for $d$ large, $n$ large relative to $d$, and $G$ connected with $n$ vertices and minimum degree at least $d$, $\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{T}\cong T)\le n^{-\Omega(d)}$ for every tree $T$, hence $G$ has at least $n^{\Omega(d)}$ non-isomorphic spanning trees; this is optimal up to the constant in the exponent. The optimal anticoncentration bound $\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{T}\cong T)\le n^{-(1/2-o_n(1))(d-1)}$, conjectured by the authors, would only give $n^{(1/2-o_n(1))(d-1)}$ non-isomorphic spanning trees, whereas $K_{d,n-d}$ has $\Omega(n^{d-1})$ of them; the authors conjecture that this larger quantity is an essentially optimal lower bound for all such $G$.
